Baby O

[DR A] (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Re-examination by MR DRIVER
Witness statement of DR OLIVER RACKHAM (read)
DR DEWI EVANS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Re-examination by MR JOHNSON

Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON

Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby O] (read)
Wednesday, 15 March 2023
(In the presence of the jury)
Yes, Mr Driver.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: [DR A] (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
[Dr A], could I invite you to state your full name for the recording, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Dr A], as I'm sure you appreciate, you're still bound by the oath or affirmation you took when you first gave evidence and you are here today to provide evidence in relation to the baby [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For your information, because the timetable, as you appreciate has been a little disrupted, the jury have already heard a statement read from your former colleague [Dr D]. Dr Cooke has already given evidence and yesterday both Drs [Dr B] and Brearey gave evidence. So although your statement deals with a lot of [Baby O]'s clinical history as dealt with by some of those doctors, that evidence is already before the jury.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So if I may, I'll move immediately to your first dealings with the baby and invite Mr Murphy to put up tile 165 and click on to the original document, please, which records how at 12.10 on 23 June -- if we could scroll down to the middle of the page, please -- you, together with your colleague, [Dr B], reviewed a cranial ultrasound that had been undertaken on baby [Baby O], I think the previous day. Do you recognise your note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was the consequence of that review?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The images that were captured as part of the ultrasound are printed off. We'd looked at those, there's a set pattern of images that is taken, and [Baby O]'s cranial ultrasound was normal. What we were looking for particularly was any evidence of haemorrhage or any evidence of dilatation of the ventricles which would be abnormal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So there are set markers that you seek out but they were absent --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- in this case? Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's 12.10 on the 23rd. I'm going to move now to 13.15 hours on that same date. Mr Murphy, if you could please take us to tile 168 and click on the middle page for now.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It would seem that at that point you were asked to see [Baby O]. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you remember who and how you were asked to see [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, I don't, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall why you were asked to see [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There were concerns that his abdomen was distended and that he'd vomited. The reason for being asked to see him would be that that vomiting was unusual.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could go back, please, to tile 167 so we can provide some context to this vomiting.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We're now going to look at the neonatal unit fluid balance chart, paper copies of which the jury have.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We are not going to dwell on it very long so we'll just use the screen for now.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Your note informs us, and we'll look at your note in detail in a moment, that your invitation to see [Baby O] was taken up at about 13.15 hours. So if we look at the feeding regime that preceded that, we can see that at 10.00 and 12.00 hours he, [Baby O], was provided with donor-expressed breast milk that was given to him via a nasogastric tube and we can see the quantities and the running aggregate amount.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look down at the bottom of the page, we can see the initials of the nurse who has recorded those feeding events.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr Driver.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There's a very annoying clicking sound coming from somewhere.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think it might be me leaning against this screen.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: No, it's not, it's coming from over here.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)
You can't hear it? It's just me, is it? It's very distracting for me, I'm afraid.
(Pause)
Anyway, the clerk has very helpfully solved the problem. Sorry, it was just distracting me.
Not at all.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It's resolved.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So [Dr A], we can see the record of [Baby O]'s feeds at 10 am and noon that day. Before we look at your note in detail, if we could go then, please, to tile 169, Mr Murphy, and if we look at the corresponding nursing note. If we look at the original document, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look to the upper left, please, we can see a reference to you, [Dr A], reviewing the patient at 13.15 hours, it having been reported to you, and does this accord with your memory, that [Baby O] had vomited undigested milk?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That is an entry made by Nurse Letby. Having looked at the fluid balance chart, having looked at that nursing note, does that serve to prompt your recollection as to who it was that asked you to review [Baby O] this afternoon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So next, if we go to your original clinical note then, which is at tile 168. That's your handwriting, I anticipate, towards the bottom of the page?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The opening line is self-explanatory. You were asked to see the patient re vomiting and does that say "abdominal distension"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It does.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You thereafter, as was your practice -- do you set out the relevant history?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's a summary of the events because I hadn't seen [Baby O] earlier than that day.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you appraise yourself of the feeding regime?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see that data and then we get to the line that begins "trace aspirate". Could you help us with the rest of that line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Certainly. So it's a trace of aspirates recorded from the NG tube, but they were -- I've put there "no bile".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this was milk or undigested milk but without any green colouring that would suggest that fluid had passed back up from the next part of the digestive tract.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. What does the use of the word "trace" in this context inform us of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That it's not a significant volume. So when a syringe is attached to the NG tube and a volume of -- or are pulled back on that syringe, a trace of aspirates is pulled back into the syringe rather than a large volume of sitting milk.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. The next line, is this a continuation of your note of things as reported to you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what was reported to you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: One vomit post-feed, so there's no indication of the time since the feed there, but that will have been as it was told to me when I went to see him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. In this context the use of "vomit", is that of any significance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It suggests that [Baby O] has expelled the milk rather than it just sort of trickling out of his mouth as a normal posset.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So something more significant than reflux, for example?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is this in itself an unusual or exceptional event in a baby on day 3 of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It could be, but it can also be normal. That's why I was asked to see him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's just complete the report as received by you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So no blood PO or PR. So none has come up through the digestive tract, either through the NG tube or in the vomit and he had passed no blood per rectum into his nappy. There's a small meconium plug at the anus. So [Baby O]'s now 3 days old and the meconium, which is a sort of hard tarry stool which is usually passed fairly quickly after birth, will have been slightly delayed in [Baby O] because he wasn't fed, he was put on IV fluids initially. The fact that he's passed meconium tells me that his digestive tract is open and working.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And his gut is moving?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could continue, please, to consider the rest of the note or is that the extent of it behind this tile, Mr Murphy?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The last bit of the previous page was the initial observations.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "On examination", I think. You just passed over the first part.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I did and I was in error to do so.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So "on examination". So now we've moved from report received to observations made?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And they were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: His heart rate is elevated, it's 160 to 170 beats a minute. I would expect [Baby O] to be 150 or just below. His oxygen saturation, I'm assuming in room air at this point, is normal at 100%. His femoral pulses are palpable on both sides of his groin, suggesting that his cardiac output is normal and his respiratory rate is 40 breaths per minute, which may be slightly elevated but not unusual. His temperature is normal for a baby in an incubator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, Mr Murphy, stay where we were. Let's deal with those features in turn. So cardiologically, what was your assessment?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: His heart rate is elevated and I don't yet know why.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This could be because he's just had a vomit. It could be because he's sore, with some sort of acid reflux following that vomit. It could be the herald of an infection starting. There could be another cause.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's why I'm there to examine him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was your overview of the respiratory position at the time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: His respiratory rate is slightly elevated. I would have expected him to be at about 30 breaths per minute just now. Again, this is shortly after a vomit and this could just be him settling back down.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The capillary refill time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Less than 2 seconds. As pressure is placed on the skin, it refills normally and it suggests that his blood pressure and fluid status is normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So considering all of those observations globally, at this stage was there anything in particular to provide you with concern?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Based on those observations there, I would like to know why he's got a fast heart rate. I would like to know why that respiratory rate is elevated. But I think I lead on to that on the next page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Indeed. Let's progress through the note then. Did you then examine his abdomen?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I did.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What did you find?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It was distended, as I was asked to see him, that was one of the reasons. His umbilicus is normal, there's no flare or erythema at the umbilicus. Redness around the umbilical cord or the stump or... a little bit like a gas flame. If you were to see something that looked like a flame-shaped discolouration around the umbilicus that would suggest that there's infection at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's something that you particularly look out for.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And in that regard what did you find?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It was normal. He had no hernias on either his femoral sites or at his umbilicus, and his bowel sounds were normal. His liver, kidneys and spleen were not unusual in their palpation, they felt normal.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So as part of this abdominal examination, you palpated, you pressed around those vital organs, you tried to seek out enlargements?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But there was none?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Next, I believe you've given your shorthand overall impression.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: One of the things with abdominal distension and vomiting, especially in a young baby, would be whether this represented the early signs of necrotising enterocolitis, so an infection, inflammation of the gut.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There is a staging system for it and observation of [Baby O] and the physical parameters that are measured on his examination suggested that that was unlikely. He didn't quite reach the first stage of the Bell score.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My impression is this was most likely distension, secondary to passing a meconium plug, and he'd had one so far, there may be a little bit more to pass.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's take those in stages. The Bell score, is that a set of established parameters against which --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- you measure a baby's presentation to seek or to enable you to arrive at a preliminary diagnosis for NEC?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Which would then start you on a treatment course, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His symptoms didn't take him very far up that chart?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No. They were suggestive of it, but not yet at a point that you would act upon it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Why is it that the passing of a meconium plug might cause abdominal distension?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So in order to pass any stool that's sort of solid or firm, extra effort and extra pressure is required and he may have been taking large breaths in order to then splint his diaphragm so that he can get extra pressure to push that stool out. He may well have swallowed some of that air.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that any more complicated than straining?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Not really.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Whilst we're with his abdomen, at that point did [Baby O] have a UVC central line fitted; can you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, he didn't have one at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So having reviewed him in this regard, what were your conclusions and what actions did you deem it necessary to take?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I'd been asked to see him so there was obviously some level of concern about how he was looking at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So my plan was to do a blood gas now and then there are some criteria set out below that if he has temperature instability, if he has apnoeas, pauses in his breathing, or episodes of
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: bradycardia, blood in his aspirates or passing it per rectum, then it would be time for an abdominal X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So first instance, take a blood gas. Secondly, conditional upon other indications of problems, X-ray?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the blood gas was taken, we can see, because there you have listed, I assume, the results of that blood gas test.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Taking them in the stages. The pH value?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's lower than expected. I was expecting that to be above 7.25. Carbon dioxide is again -- it's on the higher side of normal. Again, I wasn't expecting that, especially with a respiratory rate of 40 breaths a minute. I would have expected him to be blowing off that carbon dioxide with that increased respiratory rate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Taking those two readings together, what did they inform you of or concern you about?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby O]'s blood is more acidic than I was expecting and the combination of factors below lead to that and it's now a case of working out why that is the case.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Bicarbonate is the next line. That's okay, it's on the lower side of normal but it is okay. His base excess, which is the measure of how much he's compensating, is greater than I expected. It's normally between minus 2 and plus 2.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His glucose is normal but his lactate is elevated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The lactate is suggestive of a metabolic component to that gas. I would normally expect the lactate to be no greater than 2.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So looking at it, the gas results globally, where did they lead you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The elevated lactate and the raised base excess suggest that there is a degree of underfilling, so [Baby O] now has a 10ml per kilogram bolus of normal saline and will then be started on IV fluids. And based on that gas, rather than waiting for the criteria set out above, now is the time for that abdominal X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there at this stage, prior to an abdominal X-ray, an identifiable cause for these imperfect gas results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was your working case management thesis at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So at this point [Baby O] has a metabolic acidosis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In the short-term I can remedy that with a fluid bolus.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't know what's precipitated that. So it's time to do a little bit more. And I think we come to that next.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I think we'll see that at tiles 191 and 192. If we click on 192, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does this tend to show that antibiotics were provided?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would that have been, in [Baby O]'s case, a second line of antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: They are because he was started on antibiotics -previously on antibiotics because of his prematurity.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And that first line of antibiotics, because of prematurity, is that just a standard conservative management approach of preterm babies?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There will have been a reason for starting them and that may have been, in not [Baby O] but in either of his siblings, but because they had all shared a common blood supply prior to delivery, if one is started on antibiotics shortly after birth then the other two receive the same treatment and screening.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Forgive me if it's an invitation for you to state the obvious, but what would be the purpose of introducing second-line antibiotics to [Baby O] at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Metabolic acidosis with some queries about abdominal distension. My concern is that this is an early infection, be that necrotising enterocolitis or something else that's not declared itself yet. So start these antibiotics and then go looking for the cause.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Clinical indication: sepsis [query] cause" we can see there.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So you're just being cautious?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: Absolutely. It's preferable to start the antibiotics early and then stop them rather than not start them early enough and regret it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So that was your examination and response at around 13.15 hours on 23 June. At that stage did you feel the need to move [Baby O] from where he was currently being housed or did he remain where he was or can't you recall?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I know that he moves from nursery 2 to nursery 1 at some point. I don't recall whether it was after this event or after something else.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I think we may reach it in due course. Let's move forward in time then to 14.40 hours and, on our presentation, tile 199.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Click on the middle tile for the moment. We can see that our summary of your note indicates that you were called to see [Baby O] at around 14.40 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Of course we'll look at your clinical note in a moment, [Dr A]. Before doing so, do you have any actual memory of the circumstances that took you to [Baby O]'s side at this point in the afternoon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't remember being called, but I do remember walking with the incubator from nursery 2 to nursery 1. I think I was controlling his airway at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So you recall a feature of attending upon him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But you don't recall precisely why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Or how?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's look at your note behind this tile then, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a long note. It goes over more than one page, which has entries, if we look to the left column for the moment, that are recorded as per rather precise times over the next hour or more.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, we could leap tile to tile, but it probably makes better sense to stay with the page and as and when I will make reference to the corresponding tiles if anybody cares to note it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think that will be more helpful, so we've got a narrative, and if you would make the references as well so people can note them if they choose to.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So you were called to see [Baby O]. How was he upon your arrival?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I was called to see him at approximately 14.40 because of desaturation and low heart rate and a mottled appearance. He was bagged up, he was in the Neopuff circuit, and transferred from nursery 2 to nursery 1 but he required continual breathing support on that moving.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: That was the bit that I recall. He required 100% oxygen to maintain normal saturations at that point. His heart rate was between 80 and 90 beats per minute and I would have expected that to be usually greater than 130, 130 to 150. That's in contrast to his high heart rate an hour and a half beforehand.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Using that Neopuff circuit in 100% oxygen we were maintaining saturations of only 50% to 60%. The oxygen was increased to 100% with an increased pressure or an increased inflation pressure on the Neopuff circuit and I would say a slightly increased expiratory pressure on the Neopuff circuit. Cefotaxime had been given and the 10ml/kilo bolus of normal saline been given and a further 10ml/kilo bolus was decided upon there. That takes us as far as 15.03.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It does. So let's pause there and review that entry and the events that you have recorded. Do you recall who was present with [Baby O] when you attended upon him or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I recall there was a student nurse and Nurse Letby.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were they in the nursery with [Baby O] or elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: In nursery 2, I recall. That bit is a little bit fuzzy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly I remember moving from nursery 2 to nursery 1, but the bit just into nursery 2 is a little vague, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Could I ask you just to keep your voice up.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You're quite softly spoken.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Don't rely on the microphone. Natural voice.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR A: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Why is it that you deemed it necessary for [Baby O] to be transferred from one nursery to another at this juncture?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So [Baby O]'s needing 100% oxygen, he's needing active support with his breathing, and he's got a low heart rate that's not normal for a three-day-old baby. He needs more intervention and it's likely that he's going to need intubating and mechanical ventilation. That needs to be in an intensive care setting.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you at this point, at around 14.40, obtain a measure of the level of desaturation and the extent of bradycardia?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Only the line there that says:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Heart rate 80 to 90, sats 50 to 60."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And on the great scale of things, how significant a fall in heart rate and a reduction in desaturation are those?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Left without intervention, this is a peri-arrest event.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Would you define peri-arrest?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This will lead to a cardiac arrest, a stop in circulation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As to the mottling or mottled, as recorded in your note, are you able to expand upon that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No. It's unusual compared to the previous time that I'd seen him. So previously he'd had abdominal distension but no mottling, and at this point, an hour and a half later on, his skin looked unusual. With that low heart rate and low oxygen saturation, that may well be a cause for the mottling because he will be trying to conserve oxygen for essential organs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So he being in a state of peri-arrest, no doubt your response was an urgent one?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And I know you've taken us through the data but could you tell us in terms what that response was at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I will have been at the head end of the incubator, the perspex lid will have been taken off the incubator, and I will be supporting his airway. So I'll be using my left hand to put his neck in the right position, I'll be doing a little bit of jaw thrust with a second finger just to bring his jaw up and pull his tongue forward, and in my right hand I'll have the Neopuff circuit which I'm stabilising with my left thumb and forefinger and I will be actively squeezing the bag, delivering 100% oxygen.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was this being done as he was wheeled from one nursery to another?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, the oxygen cylinder on the incubator will have been connected until we can get him to nursery 1 and use wall oxygen again.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Does that effectively take us to your note timed at 15.03?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which, if anybody cares to make a note of, which event features behind our tile 205, but we'll stay with this page. So the entry at 15.03, which records the intubation, are these events that took place now in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So did it begin by the provision of pre-intubation medication?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So morphine, atropine and suxamethonium, as was the scheduled intubation drugs in the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were they designed to provide comfort to the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Sedation and muscle paralysis so that the tube can be inserted, again without resistance from [Baby O] and with a degree of comfort and sedation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Your note suggests that you were successful at the first attempt.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you tell us about the size of the tube and the position of the tube, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's a 3.0 diameter Portex ET tube. Portex is the brand. It's secured at 7.5 centimetres, measured at the lips. The tubes have centimetre/half-centimetre indicators on the side and the tube clamp will have been locked at 7.5 centimetres and then the ties from a ventilator hat will have then been secured to the clamp.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you satisfied as to the appropriateness of the tube size for the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The tube's appropriate for a baby of that age and weight. There will always have been alternative size tubes prepared, ready just in case his anatomy was unusual, but a 3 is perfectly sufficient. Once that tube was in, I suspect prior to it being secured, the capnograph was put just on to the little blue connector at the end of the tube, which then shows a colour changes as carbon dioxide passes through it. It confirms that it's in the tubes to the lungs and that it's -- carbon dioxide is being exhaled through it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So two tests for the same thing. The position as to the lips, ie 7.5 centimetres, is what you expected --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's calculated on his age and his weight.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But the proof of the pudding, as it were, is the capnograph?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right -- that and listening for air sounds.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which you did --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- via your stethoscope, did you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. So good colour change on the capnograph and good bilateral air entry on auscultation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it shows that both lungs are functioning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Looking at all those factors together, what was your assessment as to this intubation process?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The intubation has been fairly seamless, without having to try again and again. On the first attempt the tube is secured,
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: he will be connected to the ventilator, and at that point I will have waited for usually half an hour or so and then done a blood gas just to check that that ventilation is adequate. Again, minute by minute alterations will be made to how much oxygen is required. That's usually left to the nursing staff to make those alterations.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you attend upon [Baby O] continually? As we go through your chronology here, can we read that, between the times that you were with him, at all times?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I think after this intubation attempt, I will have gone to speak to [Baby O]'s parents. They were on the post-natal ward that sits above the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I will have explained that there's been a deterioration, he has been moved back to nursery 1, and commenced on a ventilator whilst we're waiting for investigations to sort of provide some results.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In terms of your assessment of [Baby O] and therefore the nature of your communication with his parents, what was the terms of that assessment and the tone of the communication that you were sharing with them?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So I will have explained that this is not an expected event but it's not unusual and that he's now commenced on second-line antibiotics and he is being supported for breathing with more observations being taken of his usual parameters. I will have reassured them as much as I can that this is not an unusual event, but I will have also explained that we're not in the same place that we were at the time of the morning's ward round. Again, it's a fine line between giving information and falsely reassuring or upsetting them, which may -- in 36 hours there may be negative blood cultures and he's just ridden this out.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We can see from your next entry, timed at 15.51, which in isolation appears behind our tile 219, but we'll stay with this page, that you record that you were fast-bleeped to the intensive care unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall receiving that fast-bleep notification?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I do.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In what circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I was walking -- I'd come downstairs from speaking to [Baby O]'s parents and I was walking back towards the neonatal unit and I met [Dr B] in the corridor as we were going and I briefly updated her as to what had happened prior to me going up to speak to [Baby O]'s parents. And as we were discussing that, the crash bleep went off and the voice message was along the lines of, "Neonatal arrest: attend the neonatal unit".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll come to your note in a moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you confirm that when making your witness statement in regard to these events you also appraised yourself of a note made by [Dr B], which covers the same events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, and I think the documentation for this, the events from here, was a combination of mine, [Dr B]'s, and I suspect that Dr Brearey may also have made some notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If anyone here cares to note [Dr B]'s corresponding notes, which we considered yesterday, they are behind tile 218. We'll stay with [Dr A]'s note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You were fast-bleeped to the intensive care unit and no doubt responded as quickly as you could?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What did you discover upon arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So [Baby O]'s oxygen saturations were down to approximately 35% with a corresponding drop in heart rate. Listening to him, he had good air entry. As I have not made any note that it was unequal, I will assume that it was good air entry on both sides of his chest.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can I ask you to keep your voice up again, [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Sorry. Then the Neopuff circuit had been attached to the tube and he was being bagged through the tube with minimal success.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And at 15.58, he was given a morphine bolus and the endotracheal tube was removed and I re-intubated with the same size tube to the same distance with good colour change and I have done that to ensure that there was no mechanical problem with the ET tube.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's deal with that in its component parts if we may.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The fact that you've recorded he was being bagged through the ETT tends to suggest that he had been removed from the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Had that occurred before or after your arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I suspect it will have been done before my arrival, but I can't say for sure.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Are you able to say whether the desaturation to 35% or thereabouts, whether that desaturation occurred before or after he was removed from the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: From that note, I can't say, but I would suppose that if that desaturation had been ongoing, just to exclude a problem with the ventilator tubing or the ventilator itself then he will have been removed from the ventilator circuit and attached to the Neopuff circuit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There's much more manual control with a Neopuff and you get to actually feel the resistance through the tube.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And likewise with the associated bradycardia?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The bradycardia will have followed the desaturation because there's not enough oxygen to sustain a normal heart rate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Understood. He was bagged through the tube. Did you do the bagging?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It doesn't say there who was doing it. It would have been natural for me to move to the head end of the baby and take over the airway, so I suspect that he was being bagged by the nursing staff in nursery 1 and that I will have moved myself to the head end so that I can take over there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you expand upon the phrase "with minimal success"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby O] had required rather larger than normal pressures on the Neopuff circuit when he was moved from nursery 2 to nursery 1. I will have looked at the ventilator settings -- and that's just the paragraph above -- that he'd been set on a pressure of 24/5 and if that ventilator pressure hadn't been adequate to deliver oxygen to him, I'm likely to have increased the pressures on the Neopuff circuit in order to open that chest up a little bit more with each inflation breath.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. A further dose of morphine was delivered.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was the purpose of that, the objective?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: If [Baby O] was unsettled or fighting the ventilator, an extra bolus of morphine will work quickly to sedate him more. At this point I'm obviously planning to remove the tube and reintubate him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do we necessarily read into that that he was unsettled and/or fighting the tube or was that --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It's quite likely. That would be the reason for doing it. If he'd been perfectly settled and flat there would be no need to administer any additional sedation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For the court's note, that morphine bolus is also recorded behind our tile 221.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's move on to your note at 16.01, which also features behind tile 223 but we'll stay with this page.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The ETT was removed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you explain why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The ET tube is the interface between the ventilator and the baby. It is susceptible to becoming blocked with secretions. It's susceptible to kinking or bending.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The plastic of an ET tube is flexible but it's semi-rigid and it naturally has a slightly curved shape to it. So my presumption will be that there are secretions that have been in the lungs or in the mouth and they have been sucked on the exhalation part of the breath up into the tube and then coated or lined the inside of the tube. The easiest thing to do here is remove the tube and replace it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, I'm sure everyone is on to this, but where your note simply reads "ETT removed and reintubated", that would be re-intubated with a different tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall whether you actually examined the tube that was removed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I know that I wanted to examine the tube that was removed. I don't think I had the opportunity to do it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think as the rest of the resuscitation progressed, waste kit was disposed of in clinical waste bags.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Normally, if this was not progressing on to a further resuscitation, it is common practice to look at the removed tube and comment on whether you can see a blockage with secretions or anything else, blood occasionally.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But in this case you're simply not able to assist the jury as to whether there was a blockage --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- or a distortion of the tube or any of the other factors that you've already informed us were of potential interest. So the re-intubation process was again successful at the first attempt. Same size tube and to the same position as before. What were the indicators as to how well or otherwise that tube was functioning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Again, the little capnograph that goes between the tube connector and the ventilator or the Neopuff circuit was attached and there was good colour change. I put, "Capnograph colour change [tick]".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So carbon dioxide on the way out and, you having satisfied yourself that this kit was all correctly in place, did you then reattach the kit, and therefore [Baby O], to the ventilation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes. I have said that we've recommenced continual mandatory ventilation at the same settings, so he will have been back on 24/5 with a rate of 60 breaths a minute. And as he's connected to the ventilator, there's good air entry on both sides of his chest.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So albeit with mechanical assistance, all the indicators shortly after 16.01 would tend to suggest that his respiration is functioning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did you remain with [Baby O] at this point or...?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I will have been present in nursery 1. That will have been for a number of reasons. I will have had to have -- the morphine will have been given, I presume, as a verbal instruction. That will have then needed prescribing. There will have been tidying up to do from the bits and bobs of kit that were left around afterwards, and also I will have wanted to keep an eye on him.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see there is another note made some 14 minutes later, timed at 16.15 hours, which event is behind our tile 224,
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: but again we'll stay with this page. Tell us what happened 14 minutes or so after his reconnection to the ventilation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: We have another episode of bradycardia and desaturation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby O]'s heart rate had fallen to 60 beats a minute and his oxygen saturation was down to 50%.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You told us earlier in your evidence that readings in that range are indicative of a peri-arrest?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So how did you respond?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby O] was again taken off the ventilator, the ventilator circuit was disconnected from the ET tube, and he was then hand ventilated using the Neopuff circuit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that for the same reasons as you indicated earlier, that it just gives you a better feel?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And more control?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is the remainder of the doctor's note behind this tile, Mr Murphy, or do we have to move? And if so, let's move to tile 228, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We've simply gone overleaf to the next page of your clinical notes here, [Dr A]. So it's effectively a continuation of your note of events timed at 16.15, which you left off informing the reader that you were hand ventilating him using the Neopuff circuit. How was he presenting at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: [Baby O] still had a heart rate of 60 beats per minute and 60 beats per minute is where chest compressions or cardiac massage would be started; that was started at 16.19. Following that, then adrenaline was given twice at 16.22 and 16.26. Then I go on to document other medication that's given over the next 10 minutes or so.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So in those five lines -- four lines, I should say -are you informing us that the resuscitation process kicked in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you the only medic on hand at this point, can you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No. So I... I think I recall that I was still at the head end of the incubator. I will have been taking care of the airway and the bagging. [Dr B] was still on the unit and I recall that Dr Cooke was still around, but I don't recall exactly where they were placed as this event over 4 or 5 minutes took place. If they hadn't been there then they would have been called to come as a matter of urgency.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know from the last page that this episode, the beginning of this episode, was timed at 16.15 and we can see your various notes as to when compressions began, ie 16.19, when the adrenaline was given, 16.22 and 16.26, sodium bicarbonate 16.30, at which there was some improvement, I think you'll tell us, at 16.30; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was noteworthy at 16.30?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At 16.30 [Baby O] had a spontaneous return of his circulation, so his heart rate was picking up and he was no longer needing chest compressions. At that point he was still noted to be poorly perfused. So he had a cardiac output that was measurable and because of that poor perfusion, he was given another fluid bolus of 10ml per kilogram of normal saline; that was given at 16.47.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we look at the note that says, "Spontaneous circulation", could you read the third word on that line, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: "Re-established."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Re-established. Does that imply that it was lost or that it was poor and then improved?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: In order to start chest compressions, that can be done at -- the indication to start is a heart rate of 60 beats per minute because that won't supply adequate circulation and perfusion to the baby's organs. The restoration of spontaneous circulation means that the heart rate had picked up above the 60 beats per minute and was heading in the right direction. Even though that spontaneous circulation had been re-established, he was still noted to be poorly perfused, so there is always that worry that this is a short-term restoration in part due to the two doses of adrenaline and the small bolus of sodium bicarbonate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And is that sodium bicarbonate -- is that your note at 16.47?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: No, the sodium bicarbonate is given at around 16.30.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Apologies. Then at 16.47?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Another fluid bolus of normal saline.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that to seek to address the poor perfusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At this point in the sequence of events, how was [Baby O] as a consequence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: He was in a better position than 16.19. So he was now maintaining his own heart rate and even though he was looking poorly perfused, interventions had been put in place that will take a few minutes to see how he responds, and we are certainly heading in the direction for him to be returned back on to the ventilator and the resuscitation effort is ready to stand down.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What other measures were deemed necessary at that point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So a period of time will be left before performing another blood gas. His perfusion will have been poor over the last 15 minutes and a gas will need to be done in about half an hour to an hour's time. I think, collectively, we've had a look at [Baby O] and realised that his venous access is not going to be adequate for a further attempt or a further deterioration, so whilst he's stable now is the time to get more venous access in place, which is the next part that we come to.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And why would it have been deemed desirable to get further venous access?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Over the last 15 minutes, [Baby O]'s had two doses of adrenaline, one of bicarb, and a fluid bolus. I suspect he only has one cannula in place at this time. If that one goes then there is no way of administering venous medication to him. This is the time to get ahead.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So these interventions are best done whilst the baby is stable?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So what was done in that regard?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: There are three attempts made for further venous access and the left great saphenous vein is cannulated by [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that by the ankle?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is. Following that, [Baby O] is returned back to mechanical ventilation and despite -- knowing that it's going to be a poor gas, we had been unable to get any sample for a blood gas measurement at that point.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, can you explain? Knowing that it's going to be a poor gas, unable to... Help me with that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Because [Baby O]'s ventilation has been poor over the previous 15 minutes, it is likely that his blood gas will have a low pH, even though his carbon dioxide may now be back to normal, but what will be of interest and of note here is what is his lactate doing. If that lactate has gone up compared to the previous lactate then this is indicative of more of a metabolic cause.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Where it reads:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Blood gas unobtainable on several attempt."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What was unobtainable?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The sample for the blood gas measurement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So blood?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: The blood, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Blood was unobtainable. Is that a reflection of the state of his circulation at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: It is. That again goes back to that poor perfusion noted at around 16.30. Because of that, preparations are made for an umbilical venous catheter to be inserted.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know from your evidence earlier that there wasn't a UVC. You confirmed preparations were made. Was a UVC inserted?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I don't recall whether it was managed or not.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, I'm invited to invite you to keep your voice up, [Dr A].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Your next and final entry on this page, does that effectively invite the reader to consider Dr Brearey's note from here on in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you recall why it was that you broke off from recording events at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: At this point I will have been going to find all the equipment necessary to insert and secure the umbilical venous catheter. So that will have been a move off to one of the storerooms to collect all of the sterile kit needed for that insertion and it will have been also to get all of the gowns and drapes needed to make this ideally a sterile procedure.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And are you aware of any note that suggests that that procedure was in fact undertaken or did events overtake it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: I suspect that events overtook it. It would be impossible to do a further resuscitation whilst trying to insert a UVC.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And do you recall any further direct personal involvement in any resuscitative attempts in response to [Baby O]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, so there was another collapse following this event, but I would have to read Dr Brearey's notes to sort of give you any indication of my part in that.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were you a participant in that regard together with Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: And [Dr B].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And I think Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes, I think Dr Gibbs was the consultant who will have been on call overnight and as this was after 4 pm, Dr Gibbs will have had a handover and will have come along to the neonatal unit, knowing that there was a resuscitation taking place.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, we heard from Dr Brearey yesterday in great detail about this process and I don't intend to take [Dr A] through those events minute by minute. But suffice to say, [Dr A], were you there participating until [Baby O]'s sad demise?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Having reviewed [Baby O] on more than one occasion during that day, having been with him until the very end, what, if any, conclusions did you draw on that day about those events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: This was incredibly unusual and it was unexpected. The ward round that took place at 9.30 in the morning recorded a well baby and, as the afternoon progressed, [Baby O]'s clinical condition deteriorated in a way that is indicative of a process, potentially sepsis.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe that Dr Brearey had been invited to come along in order to perform an echocardiogram on [Baby O], just to ensure that there wasn't a cardiac cause for this.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Heart malformations often declare themselves on day 3 of life, but I don't recall Dr Brearey's echo findings, if he actually had the chance to do it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Following [Baby O]'s death, did you take an interest in the subsequent blood culture results and the like?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: Those blood culture results will have taken 36 to 48 hours to reveal their results, which will have had them being available for reporting -- I think on the Saturday of that week. I may well have looked at them, but as his notes weren't open or available to write in because he was then deceased, I wouldn't have had the opportunity to record that in the notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Finally, [Dr A], in the course of the notes you made that we've considered, there's reference to X-rays. Can I just take you to two X-rays that were undertaken in relation to [Baby O] on this date. Firstly, if we could go to tile 197. We don't need to go to the X-ray itself. This X-ray, I think, is not timed or dated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But was an X-ray undertaken as part of your plan? Do you recall reviewing the X-rays on the day?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: DR A: So the X-ray machines have a small screen on them. It's for the radiographer to just check that it's an adequate position and quality of image. As this was a rapidly evolving sequence of events and I will have looked at that X-ray on the machine itself and observed that there was no air under the diaphragm indicative of a perforation and I will have reassured myself that there was nothing on the lower aspect of the chest to suggest a pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER
