blocks.text: You told us that this mark is over the area of the liver. That was in your evidence this morning.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it's under the -- sorry, if it's over the right chest wall, that's where the liver is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You have again tried to knit one piece of evidence to a mechanism to support this allegation, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I have put together the clinical findings I had in 2018 to explain what I think happened. I did not make it clear about the timing of the purpuric rash or the suspected purpuric rash and, once I got more information, I was able to give a more definitive opinion regarding the cause of this little baby's collapse and demise.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's nothing about a purpuric rash which indicates that is the site of trauma at all, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it's over the right side of the chest, and the liver is under the right side of the chest, then that's -- you can put the two together. The fact that the rash disappeared -- Dr Brearey said this -- the fact the rash disappeared in a couple of hours means it's not a purpuric rash. So whatever, it was not a purpuric rash. Okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What happened during the course of your explanation, your account (inaudible) to put it together, what happened was by the time we get to your third report on 25 March 2019, you had actually received a statement from Dr Brearey, hadn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. When you read that statement, you saw that he described how this small discoloured purpuric rash had vanished.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you realised it was impossible in that case to suggest that this is a bruise over a site of trauma; that's what you realised, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: At which point you just automatically switched to air embolus, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't automatically switch to air embolus. What I did was, having realised that this rash was a short-lasting rash and that this is something that had been published in literature, scientific papers in the past and also found in other cases in this trial, so we had this pattern of this peculiar rash and the collapse and the failure of resuscitation, so therefore this is far more consistent with this baby collapsing and dying from the effects of air embolus, but had been destabilised by trauma to the liver.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Nothing about a small discoloured rash on the right chest wall matches any description in the literature, as you put it, relating to air embolus, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm relying on what Dr Brearey said.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: No, this doesn't match any description of an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm describing what Dr Brearey described and it's not just that, it's the fact the baby collapsed and resuscitation was unsuccessful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's deal with this piece of evidence here because this is with regard to an attendance at intubation with [Dr A] round about 3 o'clock that afternoon. You're saying a small discoloured purpuric rash on right chest wall is evidence of air embolism.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. No, there's no connection between a purpuric rash and air embolism. The pattern that we have described in these
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: previous cases in relation to the discolouration in the skin, that is associated with air embolus, varies according from one case to another, but what is consistent is that it's sort of -it lasts a short time, disappears, and interestingly, I've lost count of the number of local medical staff who said they had never seen anything like this before and they have never seen anything like it since. As paediatricians we see purpura on a regular basis, so therefore there is a very unusual pattern to this particular baby's -- to this baby's particular rash, as there is to the other babies.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And once Dr Brearey -- once I received this additional information from Dr Brearey it was clear to me that the original description, ie this purpuric rash, was incorrect.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's not for the time being get hung up on the word purpuric, which refers to the blood vessel underneath and might suggest a bruise or some impact in that way.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What you are doing is taking the description that is given by Dr Brearey here and trying to convert that into something that can support an air embolism. That's what you're trying to do, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's consistent with an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: A 1 to 2-centimetre mark on a right chest wall is consistent with air embolism, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It -- well, it's not just that. The baby was in a collapsed state and failed to recover, so that adds to my clinical suspicion regarding the association between this discolouration and subsequent events, in other words, the death of this baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Let's look at this discolouration: a 1 to 2-centimetre, that big (indicating), discolouration, you say is consistent with air embolus in one part of the chest wall, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's consistent, it's part of the overall collection of diagnostic features that led to this baby's death.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You will seize on whatever you think you can to try to prop that up, won't you, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm sticking with my clinical experience and the clinical evidence in scientific papers and the fact that this baby's recovery -- sorry, demise -- and the fact that this baby died. And as we heard from Dr Brearey yesterday, he did not think that the bleeding from the liver would have been
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: sufficient to cause his death, cause his... cause his... I've forgotten the word...
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: would have made him unwell but he would have responded to resuscitation. That was Dr Brearey's opinion, I agree with it. So therefore we have, as in other cases, a combination of features here.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You endeavour to try to link what happened at 1 o'clock in the morning to what happened to the liver.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I suggest that when you got Dr Brearey's statement and read it before your report in March 2019, you saw this had vanished within an hour or two, you had to come up with something else and that's what you did?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's not a matter of coming up with something else, it's relying on the information you receive. That's what Dr Brearey says. It's up to the members of the jury to believe if what he said he saw -- you know, fine. But having read his report, he's an experienced paediatrician, he's never seen anything like this before or since, so there, that is -- and this baby died, remember, so it's... You know...
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So we can be quite clear, your expert opinion is that a 1 to 2-centimetre rash on the right chest wall is consistent with air embolus. Let me be clear: is that what you're saying? Is that right, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a feature one associates with air embolus.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: How does that fit in with good perfusion, which we know means that the blood supply and the oxygen is working well? That's part of it. Where does that fit in with good perfusion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Where's good perfusion?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This is the next words. This is material you've had for a long time. Good perfusion, how does it fit in with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If the rest of the skin looks normal then the rest of the skin is normally perfused.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That doesn't sit with an air embolus, does it, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it does actually.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You've got a 1 to 2-centimetre spot and good perfusion.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We've discussed this 1-centimetre rash, I have given you my opinion. I don't know how many times I can repeat it but that's my opinion.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Good perfusion. Is that something you encounter in the course of an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is. We've discussed this in terms of the anatomy of it. Where the air will go will vary. If the air went to a particular part of the abdomen or the chest wall, then you will find the abnormalities there.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But if the air does not go to other parts of the body then those other parts of the body will be normally perfused. That's the way it is.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. So this air embolus found a 1 to 2-centimetre spot to go to; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Throughout the whole of the bloodstream, that's where it goes to, to a 1 to 2-centimetre spot?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It can go anywhere. It can go anywhere.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You are working this together as you go along, aren't you, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I have put it all together over 5 years ago. I'm simply looking at the clinical notes without access to discussing it with local staff or anyone else. I've had to amend my view on receipt of additional information but in this case and in other cases where I have flagged up the diagnosis of inflicted injury -- right? This baby suffered from inflicted injury. In fact, he suffered three inflicted injuries in my opinion. The air embolus is one. The trauma to the liver, which I defer to the pathologist by the way, so I'm not going to go down that road, and I think the vomiting was a concerning issue as well.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So these are three separate events, all of which can be explained by inflicted injury. None of which can be explained on the basis of complications that affect stable and well premature babies.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just so it's clear --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is my view.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We're looking at your mechanisms. You have said there are three mechanisms and in fact your first one was trauma at 1 o'clock -- around 1 in the morning wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've told you about my sift reports, I've told you that I've had to add to information. This is my opinion as we are here.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Your next one is that on the basis, particularly of this mark and good perfusion, this is air embolus? That's the second one, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sticking with that. I'm sticking with that. But given that we've all confirmed that the rash was found some time in the afternoon of the day he died, a few hours before -- shortly before he died, that is consistent with the cause of his death, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's recorded at this point by this doctor when it went.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As for --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's a factual issue. Either he saw it -- either what he saw was what he saw or not. It's a factual issue.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: That's for the members of the jury to decide if what he saw is what he's described in his statement in 2019.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: As for his terminal collapse, you concluded your evidence by saying that was air embolus and gave us no particular detail. That's because it's something you're throwing in as you go along.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I am not throwing anything in at all. This is a baby who should not have died. This is a baby whose -- if his deterioration was due to one of the common causes, like infection, he would have responded to resuscitation. He did not. He was destabilised by the trauma to the liver and I think the air was what finished him off, if I could put it in that awful way.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The question --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's awful.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: -- is what is there that can make us sure that terminal collapse is due to an air embolus, Dr Evans. Right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you have identified nothing at this point that goes together to demonstrate there was an air embolus operative at that point, have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have -- the baby died, the resuscitation failed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've discussed this rash for long enough. The little baby died. I've explained how I looked at all of these cases in isolation, in other words let's not look at the other -- this is case 15, let's not look at the other 14 cases. If this was a single case and I had access to all of the information from the beginning then there would be one substantive report from me saying what I'm telling you on oath in this court today.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did not have all the information at the beginning and therefore inevitably, one amends one's opinion as a result.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You had what we see on the screen from the beginning, Dr Evans, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, purpuric rash.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We can take that down, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You have told the jury that chest compressions don't get near to the liver. That's what you have said to them.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They do not.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They don't?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, the liver --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Where is the liver in relation to the chest, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The liver is found at the bottom end of the right chest wall. Cardiac compressions are over the sternum, in other words of the middle of the -- over the middle of the chest and at the upper end of the chest wall.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: (indicating). I'm a bit bigger than these babies but the liver is here, the cardiac compression is here, and we're talking about experienced paediatricians who would know how to resuscitate little babies. And they've had plenty of experience of it, as we have heard in this trial. There's no other information I know of any other baby who had liver haematoma either as a result of chest compressions or anything else. So chest compressions will not cause --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When we come to consider this (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You have motioned towards the central area of your chest. Is that where you say chest compressions are performed on a baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I mean, I don't have a baby doll here where I could demonstrate it. Anyway, it's over the front -- it's over the centre of the chest.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm going to suggest that you well know chest compressions are performed just in the area or just below the sternum, almost over the area where the liver is or very close to that. That's where they are performed, isn't it, Dr Evans?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm not -- I know exactly where it's performed and I don't know any baby who was resuscitated by experienced people who either died and where the post-mortem showed liver trauma, as we described here, and I know of no case where babies were resuscitated successfully where cardiac compression was required but where subsequent investigation noted the liver haematoma as described here. Okay? So I don't know any of that in any case.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: What I just asked you -- it was a simple question, I apologise for having to repeat it -- was that chest compressions on a baby are performed in the area over -- just below the sternum, around the sternum or over and very close to where the liver is. That's what I asked you. Are you going to answer that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's over the top of the sternum. You're pointing in the wrong direction. It's over here (indicating) and the liver is down here (indicating), down here.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It is entirely possible for there to be some injury to the liver from vigorous chest compressions to a baby, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's very unlikely but the more important point is this: this baby collapsed, which is why he needed chest compressions in the first place. So what's the cause of his collapse? My initial view was that the collapse was due in the main to trauma to the liver, which caused the bleeding to the liver, which bled into the abdomen. That was my initial opinion because I knew nothing about this rash that had come and gone in a couple of hours.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that was -- so it fits in with the clinical impression that I had at that time. As for the early hours, the only thing I had to go on was that the heart rate had gone up, that he was in air, breathing, you know, with normal saturations. So therefore
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I looked at all the options, that doesn't fit, that doesn't -that's insufficient to explain his collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's no --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry. Therefore his collapse can only be explained for the reasons we've just discussed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Just so it's quite clear, the process as you know, is we're looking at what you're suggesting; okay?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We're exploring the basis for what you suggest as mechanisms. Do you understand that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. And I'm suggesting to you that vigorous chest compressions can cause or are capable of causing haematoma or injury to the liver.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Never seen it.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Never seen it. Are you agreeing or disagreeing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have never seen it, I have never read about it. It's not something I've heard of in any of the other babies in this series of 17 cases.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And with regard to the abdominal distension, which is the third thing you are adding, and I suggest you're putting that in as an additional feature just to try to support the allegation, aren't you, rather than to reflect the evidence?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no, it's not supporting the allegation, it's reflecting the evidence. If we look at the evidence of the abdominal distension, what we've got is that the baby, who had 13ml of fluid -- sorry, of milk, I should say, around 12.30, and there was no aspirate, in other words the rest of the fluid he had taken -- now 13ml is a tiny amount of fluid. Okay? It's a tiny amount of fluid. Half a shot. I don't drink shots, but it's a small amount. And he vomited and his abdomen blew up.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, if you've had 13ml of fluid every 2 hours and -- your abdomen isn't going to suddenly distend.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's only going to distend if you have either far more than 13ml of milk or -- and/or milk plus air.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We heard from the WhatsApp evidence the other day of the -- the WhatsApp evidence was that his abdomen blew up in the afternoon. That was the evidence from Nurse Letby in her WhatsApp thing, the abdomen blew up in the afternoon.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So you cannot explain the abdominal distension on the basis only that he had 13ml of milk.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There is --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You can not do that. If he vomited and if the vomiting was due to -- sorry, if the abdominal distension was due to milk only, then by vomiting, the abdomen would have gone down, wouldn't it? It didn't. Therefore, the abdominal distension cannot be explained on the basis of his having had 13ml of milk 45 minutes earlier.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You're a very experienced expert witness, aren't you, Dr Evans? Aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, I've been in court a lot, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Mm. Is it your belief that if you keep talking and using up time when I ask straightforward questions, somehow that will distract from my questions, I'll get bored or I'll stop asking questions? Is that what you're trying to do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's being discourteous to me and I don't think that's necessary.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You choose to hold forth upon topics at length as you like when you are asked questions, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And you choose not to answer the questions that you're asked, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There is nothing about the abdominal distension in this case that indicates, for example, an abdomen was being splinted, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I never said that, no.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's nothing about the abdominal distension in this case that shows that it was capable of or did interfere with the respiration of [Baby O], is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There was a bradycardia there, I think. I think the heart rate dropped. That's the first point. The second point, it was sufficiently concerning for a doctor to be called to attend to the baby. So it was a concerning event, okay? It was a concerning event.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There's --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, little babies will bring up bits of milk, nurses will deal with that, they won't call doctors. But this was sufficient for -- the heart rate dropped, that's concerning, the vomiting was sufficient for the doctor to be called. That's a significant event. All right?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When the doctor was called at 13.15, the event you're talking about, that was not regarded as a serious event in terms of a deterioration to be expected like the one that followed, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, which one are you talking about?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: When the doctor was called at 13.15 with the vomiting and with some abdominal distension, nobody suggested that that was an event that was going to lead to anything like this, did they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh no, they -- it was a significant event, but I would not have anticipated that as a result of that event the baby would have deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And breathing support is capable, as it happens, of causing some degree of abdominal distension, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: CPAP can lead to a bit of air going into the stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We've heard plenty of evidence in this case, Dr Evans, haven't we, about CPAP belly and distension, abdominal distension?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He wasn't on CPAP.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: He was on Optiflow.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Similar mechanism?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Optiflow is capable of causing it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It had dropped from 6 litres to 4 litres of Optiflow when this happened. Optiflow is used all over neonatal units. You don't get these sudden collapses with Optiflow.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: There is no basis to suggest that the ultimate collapse, sadly, in the case of [Baby O] arises because of abdominal distension, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, it didn't.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The abdominal distension did not cause his ultimate collapse. I've explained to you what caused his ultimate collapse. But it compromised him. That's the word I was looking for earlier. The abdominal distension compromised him.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm not going to ask any further questions, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If you can reacquaint us with the concept of a peer review, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A peer review is to look at the salient facts of the case concerned but also take into account what someone else has done before and I was asked to look at what Dr Evans had reviewed, what Dr Evans' opinion was, and to comment on whether I agreed with his opinion, whether I disagreed with his opinion, or whether I came up with a new opinion that he hadn't considered.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. You've been accused in the past in this case of simply rubber-stamping what Dr Evans did. As a matter of interest, did you agree with everything Dr Evans said in this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. Let's deal with the chronology then, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You set out the circumstances of [Baby O]'s life from his birth on 21 June through to his death on 23 June; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Taking up at your paragraph 4.5, please, on the day of [Baby O]'s death, namely 23 June, did you set out a summary of the nursing note that we have heard about at 07.32?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the consequent examination by Dr Mayberry, which was, as we know, noted in the nursing note rather than the medical records?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right. The nursing staff asked him to review the abdomen because the abdomen was described as loopy.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I heard his evidence that he was called away so was unable to write an entry.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Did you, at your 4.7, summarise what Dr Cooke had found?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, Dr Cooke undertook the ward round, routine ward round, on the morning of the 23rd, and she concluded that although [Baby O] was on 4 litres a minute of Optiflow, he was on no oxygen and had no increased work of breathing. The remainder of her examination was unremarkable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you next refer to the observation chart which the jury saw this morning before the break?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you observe what you describe as the steady increase in heart rate and respiratory rate from 01.00 hours to 13.30 hours on 23 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you refer to the fluid balance chart, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What did you find there, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That [Baby O] had been started on feeds. These had steadily increased over the course of his life, but by the 23rd he was receiving 13ml of expressed breast milk via nasogastric tube every 2 hours. And that his last feed was at 12.30 on 23 June, which was a nasogastric tube feed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Now, just pausing there for a second, if you wouldn't mind, if you could go to jury bundle 2, and go to the very final page behind divider 20, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Here we have the feeding chart, is that right, at page 23676?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can see Lucy Letby's notes of feeds given at 10.30 hours and 12.30 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And before that, we can see notes made by other nursing staff earlier in the day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it there that we see this quantity of 13ml being given every 2 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Well, early on it was 10 and it went up to 12 and then 13 --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- in accordance with the medical staff's directive that the parenteral nutrition be reduced and that the fluids be increased.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So we have heard this evidence, but just to remind us, we see towards the top of the chart the TPN, total parenteral nutrition. That, as you say, is being reduced from 2.3 down to 0.9ml per hour to nothing at all at 4 am?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And a consequential increase in the amount of enteral milk being given via the NGT while that reduction was taking place?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So to 10 to 12 and then to 13 at 08.30 hours; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do we also see that the aspirates were trace aspirates so far as the entries at 8.30, 10.30 and 12.30 were concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they say trace. Before that there's a note of aspirates but it doesn't actually give you any indication of the volume.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. I think Sophie Ellis, the jury will remember, gave us evidence about that and was asked a number of questions about that.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So taking up the chronology then. After that final feed is noted apparently by Lucy Letby at 12.30, did you note at your paragraph 4.10 an event at 13.15?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. There was a vomit of undigested milk and a development of abdominal distension.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That was what provoked Registrar [Dr A] being called and the events which he recounted to us this morning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We see then at your 4.11 that blood gases were taken; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We see that on the preceding page in the jury bundle, 23667.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can see Lucy Letby's entry there at 13.20. Can you help us with those blood gases, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The gas at 13.20 was a venous gas. The pH is low at 7.2. The CO2 is a little high in the context of a baby breathing
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: quite quickly, but is not terribly high. The oxygen, the PO2 we can ignore because it's a venous sample. The bicarbonate, again, is a little bit low. The important thing here is that the base excess is minus 8, which is higher than one would expect. So looking at that part of the gas, that shows us this baby has got a metabolic acidosis, which I think other people have spoken about already this morning.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Then moving across to the lactate, the lactate is 5.1, which is abnormal, and that would indicate that there is an untoward metabolic process going on. It doesn't tell you what's going on, but it tells us, really, that you need to take note of that and to perhaps look a bit further than you originally thought because this is an abnormal gas.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The other thing on this gas is it says here "Optiflow 4 litres" and then there's an arrow saying "CPAP" and then "air". And I actually couldn't find anything in the notes that suggested that [Baby O] had moved from 4 litres of Optiflow back on to CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: But this gas says that that's what happened. But there's nothing in the nursing notes or the medical notes to suggest that he went back on to CPAP.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So this is a note made by Lucy Letby suggesting that this child was put back on to CPAP, which isn't replicated anywhere else in the notes; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As a matter of fact, would CPAP normally, potentially, explain a distended abdomen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Potentially it would. Because CPAP is, as we've heard before, air or oxygen, so gas, blowing down the nose, it can help to keep the airways open but can also distend the gut. But it's a matter of degree, I guess. This whole concept of CPAP belly is a matter of degree. It can cause mild abdominal distension, but in my experience it does not cause severe abdominal distension.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What about Optiflow?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In my experience Optiflow does not cause a huge abdominal distension, and in fact the amount of gas put in -- the flow of Optiflow used can be quite high and so at very high levels, I guess in theory there'd be more chance of having gas going into the gut. But actually, [Baby O] wasn't on high levels of Optiflow at all, he was only on 4 litres a minute, so that would
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: not be sufficient to cause a sudden blowing up of the abdomen, as was described.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If the decision was taken to move a child from Optiflow to CPAP, is that a medical decision or a nursing decision?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's a medical decision.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So it's not a decision a nurse would be making?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, because it's a change in respiratory support. So it's a step up, it would mean that a child had required an increased amount of support, and that would not be done by a nurse on her own.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And there is no note of that in [Dr A]'s notes, is there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's no note of that anywhere else.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Moving on, please, you note next at your paragraph 4.14 that there was a profound desaturation at 14.40 hours.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that [Baby O] was described in the nursing notes as "mottled ++"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You repeat that information from [Dr A]'s perspective in your paragraph 4.15, which equates to tile 199; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At that stage [Baby O] had to be bagged with a Neopuff; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: He was bagged with a Neopuff in 100% oxygen and in fact needed high pressures in order to get some clinical improvement. [Dr A] explained that this morning: with normal pressures they couldn't actually get the saturations back, so the pressures were increased to 28/6 in order to get good saturations and chest expansion.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. At your paragraph 4.16 did you next note events at 15.03 when [Baby O] was intubated and ventilated?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's evidence that we heard from both [Dr A] and Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At your 4.17 did you next note the part of Dr Brearey's notes where he referred to a "small 1 to 2-centimetre discoloured [query] purpuric rash on the right chest wall"?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thereafter, your 4.18, and this is all in the sequence at tile 218 onwards, did you note [Baby O]'s further desaturation at 15.51?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Combined with a bradycardia?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That there was good chest movement with bagging but his saturations and condition did not improve?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, they stayed -- his saturations stayed at around 70% to 85%.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You recorded his re-intubation at 16.01; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Despite that, and despite the fact he was being given 100% oxygen, his saturations remained defiantly low, between 72% and 86%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you record next the fact that discolouration of the abdomen was also noted by the nursing staff?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, the nursing staff in their account of this particular period around the re-intubation noticed discolouration -- had mentioned discolouration of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. If we can just remind ourselves of that evidence, please, at tile 252. This is Lucy Letby's account in the nursing notes. Pretty much in the centre, it says:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Placed back on to ventilator."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So let's go just up the page. We've got the event of 14.40 with "mottled ++" and "abdomen red and distended"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. My mouse isn't working, I'm sorry. Where it says "placed back on to ventilator", it mentions, second line in on that paragraph, discolouration of abdomen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's where I was about to come to. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So four paragraphs down, as you say:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Placed back on to ventilator. Dopamine commenced."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then missing out a line, effectively, it says:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Discolouration to abdomen."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And then:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Unable to obtain heel prick blood gas due to poor perfusion."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you, at your paragraph 4.20, note that at 16.05 hours, so at pretty much the time we've just been looking at in the notes, there was a further deterioration?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And CPR was commenced at 16.19?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That adrenaline, saline and sodium bicarbonate were given?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That spontaneous circulation returned at 16.30 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And then you note:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "Perfusion was poor and the rash on the chest and abdomen persisted and is noted by the registrar and the consultant."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you have also, have you not, heard the evidence of [Father of Babies O, P & R], the father of [Baby O], as to what he saw at this time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I heard the evidence of [Father of Babies O, P & R] in court.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At your 4.21, at 16.46, did you record the fact of the X-ray and what you thought it showed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The bowel gas on the X-ray had reduced from that shown on the previous X-ray.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. That at 17.15, [Baby O]'s saturations fell to 35%?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's tiles 266 and 267.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That the rate of the dopamine was increased, he was given six doses of adrenaline, two of bicarbonate and further fluids to support his circulation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you then record the use of the intraosseous line?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the fact that, as a result of that, some further blood gases were taken, which -- are they what we can see -- if we've still got the page open in the jury bundle 2, are they the final line that we see signed by Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they are. Elsewhere in the -- obviously, on this gas it's an abnormal gas, the metabolic acidosis is much worse than the gas taken at 13.20. This says C, for capillary gas, but we know from Dr Brearey's evidence that actually it was from the intraosseous fluid. This gas was taken because they couldn't get capillary gases, which was the whole point of putting in the intraosseous line.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So this gas was taken from the intraosseous fluid.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It says lactate and glucose are unavailable, but the actual printout that is elsewhere in the notes, which is a bit like a supermarket till printout, also shows that the haemoglobin had dropped significantly by this point and was only 8.6. That's very different from the previous haemoglobin on the previous gas. So on the charts that the Countess of Chester Hospital use for the recording of blood gases, it just gives you the blood gas, it doesn't give you the other parameters that those machines are capable of giving. But actually, if you look at those, they do show a big drop in haemoglobin down to, I think, either 86 or 89.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. You referred next to the insertion by Dr Brearey of an intravenous cannula at McBurney's point?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the fact that he obtained blood from that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: He did. But as he said yesterday, only a small amount of blood. I wouldn't like people to suspect that there was a huge amount of blood there. He told us that he only obtained a small amount of blood.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Then finally, in this section, the fact that the resuscitation of [Baby O] was unsuccessful at 17.43 and, sadly, his death was confirmed at 17.47?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you next address the findings of the pathologist at Alder Hey Hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In particular, the findings concerning abnormalities, if I use that relatively neutral phrase, to [Baby O]'s liver?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And also you refer in your report, and we'll have to wait for him to hear this, to Dr Marnerides' opinion concerning the cause of [Baby O]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you consider additionally Dr Arthurs' opinion, which the jury will hear tomorrow, concerning the X-ray taken after [Baby O]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just so that the jury has a hint of what's coming, the fact that gas was detected within the great vessels of the abdomen, in other words either or both of the aorta and the vena cava?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct. He will tell you himself, I'm sure tomorrow, that he was not clear which of the great vessels the gas was in or indeed if it was both.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So can we move on, please, Dr Bohin, to your opinion and comment. Can you tell us, in the light of all that information which we've summarised, together with your reading of the records and having heard the witnesses' evidence over the last few days, what is your opinion concerning the collapses and death of [Baby O]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, [Baby O] was a slightly premature baby who was a triplet, but he was well. He was very well. He was fully fed. He was receiving minimal support and was not giving the clinical team any cause for concern until he vomited at 13.30 on the 23rd.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Although there was a trend to an increase in heart and respiratory rate, this was not thought to be significant by the clinical team treating him at that time and they decided that they would watch and wait to see what happened.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They subsequently undertook an X-ray which showed a huge amount of gas within the abdomen and my reviewing of that X-ray, and I'm not a radiologist, showed something that wasn't compatible with CPAP belly, which we have heard of before, and [Baby O] hadn't been bagged at the time that X-ray was taken, so I couldn't find an easily explicable natural reason for that amount of gas being within the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: My conclusion that the cause for that degree of abdominal distension in that circumstance was exogenous, so outside, administration of air via the nasogastric tube into the stomach of [Baby O].
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we can pause there for a second to just put a time on that X-ray. I would like the jury -- if the jury could have what we have on the screen in their papers copies that would be helpful. For your Lordship's reference it's divider 20, page 23667.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's the penultimate document behind divider 20.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we go to tile 197, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We had earlier, and the jury will recall, the explanation from Mrs Tyndall as to why this entry had been put in just before or at the time of [Baby O]'s collapse at 14.40. So it was the context of the references that caused her to put it in at this time.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So is this the image that you are referring to, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'll ask Mr Murphy to show us the image so that there's no room for mistake. This is the image the jury may recall isn't actually timed on the film.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just going back to the gas chart, please, that the jury have at 23667. This image, if Mrs Tyndall has got the timing right, is an hour and a half after Lucy Letby has written into the gas chart that this child has been put on to CPAP when there's no other evidence to support that suggestion.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. All right. So can we go back to your report then, please, Dr Bohin. I think you considered the possibilities or alternative natural cause type possibilities for excessive gas; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. There was no evidence of bilious vomiting, no other evidence that would be compatible with necrotising enterocolitis, which we have heard about this morning.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Subsequently, Dr Wright's report mentions consideration of a mid-gut volvulus, which is a condition where the actual gut twists on itself and can cause abdominal distension, but it also causes a baby to become profoundly unwell and they vomit bile and, certainly in life, [Baby O]'s presentation was not compatible with that and certainly we know from the post-mortem that he didn't have a mid-gut volvulus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. I'm sure the jury will remember that mid-gut volvulus was an issue that raised its head with the other [Baby O] in this case, didn't it, [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just going back to that X-ray then and your paragraph 5.5, did you consider "innocent" causes for what you regarded as an unusually distended abdomen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, of course I had to consider all possible causes, but I couldn't think of any cause that would cause that degree of abdominal distension and destabilise a baby that were innocent causes. So babies who are breathing quickly because they're in pain wouldn't cause that sort of distension. So I was at a loss to think of any natural, innocent causes, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. We can see as a matter of fact from the X-ray report there that, according to the radiologist Dr Wright, the NG tube was in a satisfactory position?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If that NG tube had been on free drainage, would it or would you expect it to have relieved the distension to the gut at this stage?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It depends what caused the distension in the first place. The tubes are very small, so if air or gas goes into the abdomen very slowly, if you take off the end of the nasogastric tube, the abdomen will decompress very slowly. If air is put into the abdomen acutely then it will take quite a -- well, a long time for air to come out because the calibre, the bore of the nasogastric tube is very fine, so it will only decompress very slowly if the build-up is very slow.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What was your conclusion as to the cause of this distension to [Baby O]'s stomach at this time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because I couldn't think of or find any evidence for any natural causes for this, my conclusion was that the abdominal distension and subsequent vomit was caused by excessive air put down the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. At your 5.6, doctor, do you then record the fact that in effect [Baby O] had what you've described as a series of collapses between 14.40 hours and his death at 17.47?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At your 5.7 do you record the finding noted by Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. He attended to help [Dr A] or assist, rather, [Dr A] with intubation and noted abdominal discolouration. At the time when he first saw it, he thought it was a purpuric type mark, but as it had disappeared later on that day, it couldn't have been purpuric or it wouldn't have gone.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Do you record the fact that "no detailed description of the mark" was provided by anyone?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The nursing staff mentioned discolouration of the abdomen but don't go into any detail. Dr Brearey likened the discolouration, the mark on the chest certainly, to purpura, but latterly, as he said in his evidence yesterday, he said it couldn't be purpura because it had disappeared by 17.15 and purpura would not do that, purpura lasts for days and days.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But have you now heard the description given by [Father of Babies O, P & R]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The description given by [Father of Babies O, P & R] is a very graphic description, both in the things he said and the way he gestured. Clearly the description he gave was of a rash that was coming and going. I think they were the words he used, something that was coming and going. blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: During the interview on 5/7/2018, Lucy Letby explained that she'd been the designated nurse on 23 June for both [Baby O] and [Baby P] in nursery 2.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She recalled that [Baby O] was on Optiflow for respiratory support. She was present when [Baby O] began vomiting after his feed and eventually he was moved to nursery 1, where Ms Letby continued to care for him.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby remembered that his abdomen became quite distended and how the doctors intubated him and put a drain into his abdomen. From the notes, [Baby O] had feeds at 10.30 and 12.30, which were unproblematic, apart from his tummy appearing a bit full.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said that [Baby O] was on Optiflow and that could sometimes give baby a full tummy as they could gulp in air and swallow it from the Optiflow. She would have remained present throughout those feeds, which would have taken only a few minutes. Lucy Letby thought that [Baby O] vomited and [Dr A] was called immediately after 1.15 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think "immediately after, at 1.15 pm".
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I beg your pardon.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Dr A] was already on the unit. Lucy Letby did not recall if she was present when [Baby O] vomited.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said she discovered a collapse at 14.40 hours after hearing [Baby O]'s monitor sounding.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She could not recall anyone else being present in the room at the time and, as far as [Baby O] was concerned, he was mottled all over with a red, purply, blotchy red rash and red on his abdomen.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby explained that a mottled presentation was something seen regularly in neonates, although not normally to this extent. She said the mottling could indicate infection or poor perfusion. Lucy Letby did not know whether she or another nurse called the registrar.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby O]'s final collapse was at 15.51 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was in the nursery with him at the time and [Dr A] had left to update [Baby O]'s parents.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was shocked and upset by [Baby O]'s death.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She just remembered his abdomen kept swelling up and they ended up doing a drain and an intraosseous access, which were not nice things to see. She described his death as unexpected.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby described the day as particularly busy.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The doctors were back and forth, being pulled in various directions. Usually if there was a ventilated baby, they'd be round a little bit more. Lucy Letby said each time you'd have to call the registrar to come, there's an element of delay, but she did not feel that the initial collapse at 14.40 could have been prevented.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said after the profound desaturation at 14.40 hours, it was a bit more clear that [Baby O] was unwell. He was ventilated and left by the medical team.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the interview on 12 June 2019 Lucy Letby confirmed that she was [Baby O]'s designated nurse. She could not remember if she had been left alone in the nursery when [Baby O] first collapsed. She agreed that she had administered a saline bolus to [Baby O] at 14.40 hours and that his collapse must have been within a short space of time after. She denied deliberately causing him harm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: At the time of [Baby O]'s second collapse at 15.51, he was in nursery 1. Lucy Letby agreed that she was in the nursery at that time and that [Dr A] had left to speak to [Baby O]'s parents. Lucy Letby questioned whether the damage to [Baby O]'s liver was caused during the course of resuscitation. She denied physically injuring [Baby O] and denied introducing air either intravenously or via the nasogastric tube. When asked who had harmed him, she replied, "It wasn't me".
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She couldn't recall a Facebook search for [Baby O]'s mother on the anniversary of his death in 2017 and she could not explain why she would be doing it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was reminded that on her first day back from annual leave, she'd messaged Jennifer Jones-Key to say that she would be "back with a bang". She didn't know whether Jennifer Jones- Key had said something about how busy the unit would be with the arrival of triplets.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: After [Baby O]'s death, Lucy Letby messaged [Nurse E] to suggest that the cause of death may have been sepsis or necrotising enterocolitis. She said that is what she thought at the time as it was a discussion they had all had.
